meta.title: App Audio Router — Per-app audio routing for Windows: one app to many devices, or into another app
meta.description: Free, open-source per-app audio routing for Windows 10 / 11: send one program's audio to several playback devices at once — or into another program's input — each with its own delay compensation and volume balance. No virtual audio driver.
meta.ogDescription: Free, open-source per-app audio routing for Windows 10 / 11: one application → many devices, or into another app, with per-device delay compensation and volume balance. No virtual audio driver required.
meta.imageAlt: App Audio Router routing Music.exe to a Bluetooth headset, an HDMI output and USB headphones at the same time, with its own delay and volume shown under each device

hero.title: One program's sound, to many devices at once — or into another app
hero.tagline: Per-app audio routing for Windows: send one program's sound to several playback devices at once — each with its own delay compensation and volume — or into another program's input.
hero.description: Free and open source. The whole app is a single native binary calling the Windows Core Audio API directly — routing installs no driver and no helper executable; feeding another program runs through a loopback endpoint pair you pick in Settings. Routing applies to running programs immediately, no restart needed.
hero.note: MSI / NSIS installer · Free, no ads · English / 简体中文 interface

features.title: Route, align, balance, feed
features.description: No mixer graph, no virtual cable: pick a program, pick destinations — playback devices, or another program that can take input — click once. Every capability comes from the Windows Core Audio API — nothing is installed into the audio stack.

routing.title: One app → many devices
routing.description: Select one or more processes and one or more playback devices; the audio is mirrored to all of them live. A running program never needs a restart, and stopping sends it back to the system default.

feed.title: One app → another app's input
feed.description: The same destination picker lists every program that can take sound in. It is one more destination, not a move — the source keeps playing where it did — so Discord hears Spotify the way a microphone would. Feeds run through the loopback endpoint pair you pick in Settings; until then the rule is kept and the board says so.

delay.title: Per-device delay compensation
delay.description: A signed millisecond value per device: positive holds a fast device back, negative marks the earliest one. Wired speakers and a Bluetooth headset sound at the same moment, with configurable range and step. Settings → Delay compensation → Calibrate measures it for you: each device plays short tones in turn, you tap when you hear one, and the differences are written as the compensation.

volume.title: Per-device volume balance
volume.description: A 0–100 % value per device, attenuating it relative to the loudest one in the route. Changes are pushed to running routes and are audible immediately.

level.title: Per-program level alignment
level.description: Every routed program carries its own 0–400 % level; one click brings all playing programs to the loudest one's level, no manual per-app tweaking.

memory.title: Auto-remember · live lists · fails loudly
memory.description: Routing rules are stored per executable name and restored when the program plays again. The device and process lists follow Core Audio's own change notifications on their own — no polling. If one device of a route cannot be opened, the rest keep playing and the log names the one that went silent.

scenarios.description: Every scenario below is a combination of the real capabilities above — nothing invented.

sibling.title: Keep your headphones on, let others hear too
sibling.description: The headset is yours, the speakers are for everyone else: route the player to both at once, and nobody has to take the headphones off or crowd around.

sync.title: The Bluetooth headset no longer lags
sync.description: Bluetooth codecs add inherent latency, so wired speakers and a headset never line up on their own. Give the fast path a millisecond delay and both devices sound at the same moment.

balance.title: Headset too quiet, speakers too loud
balance.description: A percentage volume per device, attenuated relative to the loudest one. The first device is driven natively by Windows; every mirrored path is tuned separately.

feed.title: Let your voice chat hear your music
feed.description: Discord hears Spotify the way a microphone would: pick a program that can take input from the same picker, it connects on the spot, with undo in the toast — routed through the loopback endpoint pair you named in Settings.

faq.title: About App Audio Router
faq.description: Direct answers from the project FAQ; the project documentation is authoritative.

free.question: Is App Audio Router free?
free.answer: Yes. It is open source under the MIT licence, with no paid tier and no account.

driver.question: Does it need a virtual audio driver such as VB-CABLE?
driver.answer: No. Routing, duplication, delay and gain are all done by the app itself, calling the Windows Core Audio API directly. Nothing is installed into the audio stack and uninstalling leaves nothing behind.

feed.question: Can it send one program's audio into another program — like letting a voice app hear my music?
feed.answer: Yes — that is the 2.3.0 addition. The same destination picker lists every program that can take sound in: pick one and it connects, the source keeps playing, and the target receives its audio as if from a microphone input. Feeds run through a loopback endpoint pair you install and select in Settings — Windows provides none by default, and this app installs no virtual driver for you; until configured, the rule is remembered and the board explains why.

running.question: Can it change the output of a program that is already running?
running.answer: Yes. Routing applies to the live audio session, so the program does not need to be restarted — a game or a browser tab keeps playing while it moves to the new device.

reset.question: After I stop routing, does the program follow the system default device again?
reset.answer: Yes — that is what 2.1.1 fixed. While a route is live, Windows stores a fixed output device for that program (the very mechanism that moves a running program's audio), and that stored device outranks the system default. Stopping the route, quitting the app, and Settings → Reset per-app output each hand it back, so the program follows the default device again, including every device you pick afterwards. Versions before 2.1.1 left the device fixed after a stop, which is why a program could keep playing to the old device — or ignore your device switches — until the reset was done.

missing.question: Why is my program not in the list?
missing.answer: A program only shows up while it holds an active audio session, so start playback in it — the list notices on its own, or press Refresh. Programs that use ASIO or WASAPI exclusive mode never create a session with the system audio engine and will not appear, and system-critical processes are deliberately excluded: a route for one is refused rather than half-applied.

bluetooth.question: Can it fix the desync between a Bluetooth headset and wired speakers?
bluetooth.answer: Yes — that is what delay compensation is for. Estimate how far the Bluetooth device lags and give the faster device that value as a positive delay (for example +180 ms). Positive values hold a device back; a negative one marks the earliest device in the route.

platform.question: Is macOS or Linux supported?
platform.answer: No. The routing mechanism is built on Windows Core Audio, so the app is Windows-only (Windows 10 and 11, 64-bit).
